en: The Second Daily Lesson of the First Chapter.
// The Section on the Characteristics of Discourse //
// Purity //
Thus, in this first chapter, the Nyāya system, together with its limbs and sub-limbs, has been defined.
And that [system], though intended for others, must be applied through detailed analysis during an inquiry conducted by a single speaker, which begins with questioning and involves counter-arguments;
and in that context, the focus is upon establishing proof (*siddhi*).

However, that which is the counter-position to the commencement of the refutation of a *nyāya*—namely, the activity called debate (*kathā*) involving the exchange of arguments among various speakers—must be investigated. And therein, its purpose is directed toward censure (*upālambha*).

Thus, the meaning of the first chapter (*āhnika*) is the definition of the constituent parts of the *nyāya*, which consists of the commencement, the investigation, and the establishment [of the thesis].

The subject matter of the second daily lesson (*āhnika*), however, is the analysis of instigation (*pravartanā*) and the definition of the categories of objects concerning censure (*upālambha*); therefore, its commencement is now appropriate.

Furthermore, since discourse (*kathā*) consists of modes of engagement by way of the person being engaged and the object to be analyzed, the section on discourse (*kathā-prakaraṇa*) is commenced first.
And although discourse was not explicitly mentioned [in the previous summary], it is nonetheless implied.
Nevertheless, fearing an inconsistency, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) classifies debate (*vāda*) and the other forms of discourse by including them within that [category of *jalpa*].

For otherwise, since the definitions of debate and so forth would not enter into the preceding or succeeding sections, they would not enter into the daily lesson (*āhnika*), with the consequence that they would fall outside the scope of the treatise (*śāstra*).
Now, why was discourse (*kathā*) not explicitly mentioned by the author of the Sūtras himself?
Is it because the general and the particular are designated according to their respective roles in accordance with the intended result—whether singular or plural?

For example, when the four [means of knowledge] are intended as the result, they are designated as "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*); yet those same [four], when intended as having twelve objects, are designated as "objects of valid cognition" (*prameya*).
In that case, it was intended merely as a refutation— [asserting] pleasure to be suffering;
but here, however, there is a determination of reality, whereas in *jalpa* (disputation), there is the demonstration of one's own power and the opponent's lack of power.
In the case of *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), the intended results are the mere demonstration of the opponent's lack of power;
and since these cannot be accomplished by mere talk alone, they are specifically singled out for mention.

In this context, having employed the word "discourse" (*kathā*) in its etymological sense, [the author] objects to the *Bhāṣya* on the grounds that it is misplaced and defective, and then resolves it with the *Vārttika*, beginning with the words "That is incorrect," and so forth.

This word "kathā" (discourse) does not depend merely on its etymological derivation (*yoga*), but rather its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is restricted to it only when that [specific condition] exists.
Anticipating the objection regarding the fault of inopportune timing (*anavasara-doṣa*), he says: "But rather... (*api tv iti*).

Now, one might object: "Investigation (*vicāra*) consists in determining the relative strength and weakness of the prima facie and final positions; and that [investigation] is not the locus (*āśraya*) of debate, but rather its subject matter (*viṣaya*. To this he says: "the subject matter of investigation.
According to the view of the eminent Gauḍa Naiyāyikas, there are four types of debate (*kathā*).
Sānātani [argues] that "vitandā is that which lacks the establishment of a counter-position," because here, like *jalpa*, *vāda* is also implied;
and because the fourth example is also applicable according to the intention of the person [who employs it].
The outsiders maintain that this path of discourse is only one;
they are refuted by one who restricts it to either two or three types.
Furthermore, it is contradictory [to claim] that there is both a discourse for those seeking to know reality and a cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).
For the determination of truth does not occur merely through the cessation of the first means of proof, since that [truth] cannot be established without a means of proof;
nor can the status of the first as a means of proof be maintained without refuting the means of proof of the opposing side.
Because they are suspicious of their opponent's position;

for if two disputants were considered successful merely by that much— without even examining the proof of the counter-position, as occurs in the case of *vitandā* (destructive criticism) among those seeking victory—
then they would not be seekers of truth.

And if it is thus that one desires victory, why not point out [the opponent's] lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*) and so forth? Furthermore, no result other than victory or the determination of the truth remains for the debate.
The purpose for which debate (vāda) and destructive criticism (vitaṇḍā) exist is the production of the determination of reality (tattvanirṇaya) where it has not yet arisen,
and the preservation of it where it has already arisen.
And there is the application of what has been protected;
that consists of both personal practice and the instruction of others out of compassion.
And all of this is concluded by three discourses; it is not to be brought to completion by a single discourse alone.
But even by this much, the general definition has not been fully elucidated; therefore, he says: "And thus...
[The compound] consists of various speakers acting as mutual objects, like a battle or an embrace.
By this, it is meant that a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*) is a composition of sentences.
This is because they stand in mutual expectancy as objects of action, and because they possess multiple purposes such as victory and so forth;
furthermore, by the prefix *pra-*, the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of the speakers is indicated.
And that consists in being the one who carries through the great discourse in the form of the debate.
Thus, those qualified for the debate are shown to be: composed, not denying the convictions of all people, relying on their own opinion alone, attentive, and not a creator of quarrels;
conversely, those possessing the opposite qualities are to be excluded.
Fearing a breakdown in the etymological derivation (*nirukti*), he says: "In discourse (*vāda*) regarding the expression of meaning.
The intention is that those who are unqualified should be excluded.

Furthermore, these five are to be accepted in discourse: one who speaks according to the subject at hand, one who is not deceptive, one whose speech is timely, one who does not raise frivolous objections, and one who possesses conviction established through reasoning; conversely, those who possess the opposite qualities are to be rejected.
Since such things are generally of the nature of poison and so forth, they alone have been mentioned.
This being the case, having abandoned what is to be discarded, that which is as it truly is ought to be spoken of as it truly is.
When this is so, there is discourse for the sake of establishing the Great Sentence, which results in the attainment of the fruit.
For those who desire to fight and those who desire to enjoy do not achieve their intended goal by acting for a long time without first establishing it;
thus, "according to the enunciation" means that because debate is the cause for the realization of reality, the enunciation comes at the beginning.
He prepares a seat for the Vārttika to sit upon with the words "tadanavasāyāt" (because of that non-ascertainment).
With the word "evam" (thus),
he states the purpose of the extended application (atideśa) with "na vicāram" (not [the need for] deliberation).
First, he excludes *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) by way of its exclusion from what is heard [in scripture], using the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
Now, he excludes *jalpa* (disputation) by way of its exclusion from the intended meaning (*tātparya*), using the words "and even though" (*yadyapi ca*).

The phrase "by means of those rooted in valid cognition" (*pramāṇamūlaiḥ*) refers to those things considered to be rooted in valid cognition; the word "necessarily" (*niyamena*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
Since no restriction regarding intention is heard [in the scriptures], he says: "And how this is so...
Furthermore, reasoning (*tarka*) requires a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing a proof, but for refutation, it is capable even when alone.

Because what is struck down by counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*) lacks probative force, he says "in both ways" (*ubhayathā*), as if anticipating the acceptance of the future [term] as having a positive probative force (*bhāvasādhana*).

As for the objection regarding that [future term], it occurs either in the very mention (*uddeśa*) of the words "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and "reasoning" (*tarka*), by means of a self-denotative indication (*svavācakalakṣaṇā*), just like the words "proof" (*sādhana*) and "refutation" (*upālambha*).
It is almost established either by being an intermediate operation of the word or by being conveyed by the word itself;
therefore, he says "But when... as if it were already proven.
For censure (*upālambha*) consists in pointing out a fault.
Furthermore, that which is insentient neither commits an offense nor is it instructed;
so too is the case with the person (puruṣa).
This is what was stated: "the reproach of [attribution] to the nature of the person.
For the primary operation belongs to the object and the instrument;
the result, however, is one and the same.
And by that means, the object [is established];
in the present context, even though there are both the object and the instrument, it is indeed the object alone.
However, this much is the distinction:
The property of impermanence belonging to sound and so forth at the time they are objects (karman) is indeed an object, even when [sound] functions as an object or an instrument (karaṇa).
However, there is this distinction:
that at the time it is an object, the impermanence of sound and so forth is a property [of that object] because it is what is intended to be known (jijñāsita).
However, intending that [the term] refers to the thing as such in its state as an object (*viṣayatva-daśā*), he explains it in accordance with the literal Vārttika as "the substratum" (*dharmin*).
Otherwise, it is also easily understood in this way: the object is the scope of the capacity, which is to say, the effect (*kārya*).
For in the Bhāṣya—"because of the application of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in this debate (*jalpa*)"—it says: "One should not harm any living beings."

The meaning is that, just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma," this is a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) that excludes all points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in debate, provided it is not contrary to the established tenet (*siddhānta*), and so forth;
this is clearly understood.

However, the author of the Vārttika [holds that] just as the eating of all five-toed animals might follow from natural inclination (*rāga*), so too, because of the mention of "objection" (*upālambha*), there would be the possibility of all points of defeat.
He [the opponent] has explained that the subsequent term is introduced for the purpose of restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*), as in the rule "five five-nailed animals are edible.
To this, [the author] replies with the word "jalpa" (disputation), showing that despite his great skill, he does not avoid mutual contradiction;
nevertheless, the claim that it is for the sake of a restriction (*niyamārtha*) remains inconsistent.

For a restriction (*niyama*) has as its result the exclusion of alternative possibilities (*pākṣikavyavaccheda*). And in this case, [defeats] such as "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*) are not among the alternatives, because they have already been definitively excluded by the word "objection" (*upālambha*). Therefore, he says: "Restriction is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)."
The meaning is this:

although it is taught that an injunction (*vidhi*) applies when something is absolutely unestablished, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally established, and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) applies when it is established both there and elsewhere.

Thus the distinction has been shown; nevertheless, thinking that this [distinction] is too slight, the term "restriction" (niyama) is also employed even in the case of "exclusive specification" (parisaṃkhyā),
because the result— characterized by the exclusion of others— is no different.

In this debate, the progression of points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is fourfold. Some are simply impossible [to occur], such as the group of six: loss (hāni), abandonment (sannyāsa), the meaningless (nirarthaka), the irrelevant (arthāntara), the unintelligible (avijñātārtha), and the incoherent (apārthaka).

Some [faults], even if they occur, are not to be pointed out, such as this group of seven: another proposition (*pratijñāntara*), another reason (*hetvantara*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*), and neglecting to question what should be questioned (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*). On the other hand, some are merely to be pointed out, such as:

The sevenfold [set of fallacies] consists of contradiction (*virodha*), mistiming (*aprāptakāla*), deficiency (*nyūna*), excess (*adhika*), repetition (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ayathānubhāṣaṇa*), and departure from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Furthermore, there is a twofold set that concludes the debate, namely: fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) and censuring what is not to be censured (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).

In that context, since [objections such as] defeat (*hāni*) and so forth consist in the concealment of one's incapacity, and since such concealment is absent in a formal debate (*vāda*) because of the desire to know the truth (*tattva-bubhutsutā*), those [objections] are impossible there.
He states the reason for not raising those [objections] when they might otherwise occur: "Indeed, not... and so on.
He states the reason for pointing out [the faults] even when one does not bring the discussion to a conclusion: "But more than that," and so forth.
Direct contradiction of the realization of truth consists in a contrary realization;

for example, when fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are not pointed out, or when an occasion for censure (*niranuyojyānuyoga*) is not pointed out. Indirect contradiction, however, is the obstruction of the causal complex for those [faults], such as distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) and the like.
In that regard, even if the first [type of contradiction] does not arise when the additional [property] is not manifested, the second type will certainly still exist.
For instance, in the case of contradiction, there is an absence of compatibility (*yogyatā*).
In the case of what is untimely (*aprāptakāla*), there is an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). In the case of what is deficient (*nyūna*), there is a failure to utter what is expected;
and that is a specific form of non-attachment (*anāsakti*).
In the case of the superfluous (*adhika*), there is a co-utterance that is not required by expectancy;
the same applies to the redundant (*punarukta*).
That too is a specific instance of the absence of expectancy.

In the case of speaking incorrectly, there is a failure to reconnect what has been said; in the case of abandoning one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*), there is the onset of contradiction by direct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). A sentence that possesses expectancy, compatibility, and contiguity, and which is not sublated by other means of valid cognition, is a factor for the realization of reality, and not otherwise.
Therefore, this [objection] should be raised for this purpose.
All of this is intended by the author of the Sūtras and is obtained from the Sūtra itself;

however, the author of the Vārttika has shown the fourfold set beginning with "deficient" (*nyūna*) merely for the sake of illustration, and has not established a restrictive rule (*niyama*). He demonstrates this under the guise of the phrase "and so it is" (*tathā ca*).
[Objection: But surely "mutual connection" (vyatisaṅga) means "exchange" (vyatihāra), and that is understood simply by saying "it possesses both proof and apprehension.
Therefore, the inclusion of the terms "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) and "reasoning" (tarka) is redundant. To this he replies: "In the former [case]..."
Nevertheless, one might ask: what is the purpose of this position? To this he says: "And for the sake of qualifying the proof and the refutation.
A *sabhā* (assembly) is said to be a gathering of people consisting of those who are to be obeyed (*anuvidheya*), neutral arbitrators (*sthayin*), and members (*sabhyapuruṣa*).
Among these, the action of the one who is to be obeyed consists of honoring or not honoring [the disputants] according to their ability and according to the rules.
This does not apply to debate (*vāda*).
For in that case, one who himself does not know reality, desiring to know it, should attend upon one who knows reality.

However, for the arbitrators (*stheya*), there is the establishment of the specific rules of the place of debate, the presentation of the prima facie and final positions, the determination of the merits and defects of the two disputants, the awakening of the defeated opponent, and the communication of the fruit of the discussion once it has been concluded in the world.
And [this applies to] the actions [of the disputants].

For this purpose, the utility of an arbiter in that context is such that the two disputants would otherwise be unable to act in this way by grasping the reasons; but it is not so in the case of a formal debate (vāda).
Intending to show that in that case, those two [the proponent and opponent] alone are capable due to their freedom from passion, he says: "not in the debate, for the sake of the judges.
Is it then that they are to be entirely excluded there?
No; he says: "but those who have arrived by chance."

The intention is that [the purpose] is to dispel the suspicion that these appear to be mere semblances of discourse resulting from negligence, and not to cause the aforementioned actions to be performed. //1//
*Jalpa* (wrangling) is the employment of means for proof and refutation through quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, as previously described. //1//
// Purity //
Because it shares the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of possessing the means of proof for both sides, the definition of *jalpa* is established immediately after that of *vāda*.
Once that is established, he states the connection [between them] with the word "definition" (*uddeśa*).
Now, one might object: since it is impossible for *jalpa* to possess the means of proof for both sides, it does not exclude *vitaṇḍā*.
For if the first argument has been refuted, then the proponent is defeated and the second party has won.
The discussion has ceased.
If it is not [the case that] he was refuted—then, whether by the statement of a fallacious rejoinder or by silence, the second party is defeated; thus, the first party has won.
[The opponent] says that [the debate] has ceased because there is no occasion for a second proof;
this is not so.
For just as in a formal debate (*vāda*), the determination of truth occurs when one's own proof is established and the opponent's proof is refuted, and not otherwise.

Likewise, in a debate (*jalpa*), victory consists in establishing one's own proof and refuting the opponent's proof; in the opposite case, there is defeat. When both [proof and refutation] are established or both are refuted, the assembly itself prevails.
Thus is the sequence for engaging in a debate: once the proponent has employed a mere proof, either briefly or in detail...

When the [proponent] has ceased after extracting the appearances (*ābhāsa*), and the stated apprehended object and refutation are not attained— that is, when the apprehended object and refutation spoken of as external to the appearances are not obtained—

the opponent, having understood the meaning of that statement, should repeat it and, after refuting it, employ a formal proof (*sthāpanā*) for his own position. However, one who does not employ such a proof, even though he has refuted the opponent's position, is not victorious.
A hero who strikes down others while failing to protect himself might be praiseworthy; likewise,

when the opponent has thus desisted and there is neither a statement nor a being-stated, neither a graspable point nor an occasion for defeat (nigrahasthāna), the first proponent— having understood that speech, having repeated it, and having identified the lack of a graspable point and an occasion for defeat in the opponent's response which was stated as a member of the refutation— should refute the part of the proof (sthāpanā).

However, one who does not find fault—even while protecting his own position—is not victorious; rather, he would be praiseworthy like one who avoids striking back after being struck by another, provided he does not strike him. But if, through the appearance of an unspoken, spoken, or graspable fallacy, or through the attainment of a defeat based on what was stated or external to what was stated, the debate ends at that very point, there is no room for further investigation of the proof.
Just as one who faints at the very moment of aiming an arrow finds the act of warding off that arrow or employing a weapon to be futile, so too is it here:
that which is to be grasped but is not stated constitutes "inability" (*apratibhā*) and the like;
that which is being stated but is not grasped constitutes "untimeliness" (*aprāptakāla*) and the like.

The "apparent" (ābhāsa) refers to what is stated as being outside [the category of fallacies], such as contradictions with one's own thesis (pratijñāvirodha) and so forth. When these are absent, there is consideration of the "apparent. Furthermore, when a counter-refutation is stated, there is the "apparent" loss of the thesis (pratijñāhāni) and so forth, which lies outside [the formal categories].
And this is to be elaborated upon in the fifth [chapter].

Although the extension of the two terms "not contrary to the established tenet" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) and "endowed with five members" (*pañcāvayavopapanna*) would be redundant—since all [points] are already included by the term "points of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) without distinction—nevertheless, thinking that it is unnecessary to resort to such a partial interpretation when the literal commentary (*bhāṣya*) is already consistent with the maxim of the "ox and the bull" (*gorbalīvardanyāya*), he harmonizes the *bhāṣya* with the *vārttika*, saying: "Merely stated," etc. Even though, for the sake of concealing his own faults, he has included among the points of defeat those such as abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the thesis (*pratijñāntara*), renunciation of the thesis (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*), a different reason (*hetvantara*), a different subject matter (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), and departure from the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Nevertheless, it is not possible to employ every means of defeat (nigrahasthāna).
Furthermore, even when there is a lapse due to negligence, it is more appropriate to counter-argue by means of quibbles (chala) and the like;
for compared to the formal points of defeat, those [quibbles] constitute less conspicuous offenses.
Therefore, the introduction of all these [objections] is solely for the purpose of being raised [as points of contention].
And thus, with the intention that they are not improper, he says: "What then?
Furthermore, the phrase "when the proponent has employed a valid means of proof" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
It should also be understood that [the opponent] has undertaken the means of proof with great effort.
Now, one might ask: "What further point is being made after refuting the Bhāṣya?
For even that [Bhāṣya] establishes that [the work] is for the purpose of protecting the truth. To this, he says: "In this manner..."
The commentary is inconsistent regarding the manner [of interpretation],
but not regarding the purpose;
therefore, that too should be understood in exactly this way.
The derivation of the *chalas* and so forth is [the purpose] by way of being employed; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. //2//
That which lacks the establishment of a counter-position is vitandā (cavil). //3//
// Purity //
Now, is it not inconsistent that *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) lacks the establishment of a counter-position?

For if there were only one side’s proof, the capacity of the person [engaged in debate] could not even be determined. Or, if that were the case, what is the use of *jalpa* (disputation), which involves such great effort?
[Objection: Ultimately, because it enters into the second proof by way of being a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*), this is not so;

for even though there is no difference in the assessment of human capacity, in *jalpa* (disputational debate), there is an assessment of capacity regarding both [parties] due to the fault of lack of reflection.
It is like the battle between two Kṣatriyas who have mastered their sciences;
whereas in the case of cavil (vitaṇḍā), it is like the battle between Daśaratha and the son of Daśānana,
or like the battle between the crow and the owl.
The capacity for self-reflection is attributed to one [type of debater], while skill in refuting others is attributed to the other.

If it is asked how this distinction arises, it is due to the intentions of the two disputants or the requirements of the adjudicator; thus, there is nothing inherently problematic here. Furthermore, the entry into the second means of proof is not prohibited because it functions as a form of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Rather, it is by way of being established;
nor is this a fixed rule, because even through the mere pointing out of a flaw— such as its being unestablished— the debate may reach its conclusion.
It is understood precisely from the force of the etymological explanation of the term itself;
nor should it be said, "Let it be so," because [the definition] would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), as the refutation of an opponent's position is already included within *jalpa* (wrangling).
If it is argued that its exclusion follows from the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*), we say no; for by that [word], the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not excluded.
This is because it is also logically consistent to define *vitaṇḍā* as merely a refutation within the context of a collection consisting of both a proof and a counter-argument. //3//
Thus ends the section on the characteristics of discourse.
// Chapter on the Characteristics of Fallacious Reasons //
// Purity //
Thus, the subject matter of the discussion has been established;
its body consists of proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa).

In that regard, the proponent of the proof must first strive to avoid fallacious proofs (tadābhāsa), and the opponent who offers the refutation must likewise strive to adopt valid rejoinders (saduttara).

Since a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is introduced before *chala* and the others for the purpose of training—on the principle that when a valid rejoinder (*saduttara*) is not obtained, one resorts to an invalid rejoinder (*asaduttara*)—the same logical connection applies here as well. Thus he says: "In the enumeration...

Here, within the sixteen-fold classification, that which is divided into sixteen by the distinction between pervading (*vyāpaka*) and non-pervading (*avyāpaka*) reasons is intended to be further analyzed according to the distinctions of unestablished qualifier (*asiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), unestablished qualificand (*asiddhaviśeṣya*), ineffective qualifier (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇa*), ineffective qualificand (*asamarthaviśeṣya*), doubtful qualifier (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇa*), and doubtful qualificand (*sandigdhaviśeṣya*).
Thus, there are one hundred and ninety-two [fallacies].

That same [set], through its relation to the proponent and the opponent in cases of non-establishment and doubt, would become one hundred and twenty-eight. That same [set], through the distinction of non-establishment for either one, and through the divisions of the fallacy of a misplaced locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*), an incapable [reason] (*asamartha*), and a doubtful qualifier (*saṃdigdha-viśeṣaṇa*) or qualified (*saṃdigdha-viśeṣya*), would constitute another one hundred and ninety-two.

That same [set] becomes another one hundred and twenty-eight due to the non-establishment of the substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relationship (*saṃbandha*).

That same [set] becomes another one hundred and ninety-two due to the non-establishment of the substratum, the qualifier, the lack of common locus (*avyadhikaraṇa*), the incapacity (*asamartha*), and the doubtful qualifier, the qualified, and their relationship.
That same [set] becomes another one hundred and ninety-two due to the doubt regarding the lack of common locus, the incapacity, and the doubtful qualifier, the qualified, and their relationship.
This same [fallacy], by adding the unestablishedness of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), constitutes another ninety-two hundred [types].
That same [fallacy], having abandoned its state of being doubtful and instead adopting the fallacy of being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*), constitutes another ninety-two hundred [types].
This same [fallacy], by adding the unestablishedness of the locus, constitutes another ninety-two hundred [types].
Excluding that very [type of] "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*) and including "contradiction" (*viruddha*), there is another one hundred and ninety-two;
and by further adding "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) to this same set, there is another one hundred and ninety-two.
Such is the detailed expansion (*prapañca*) of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
In order to elaborate upon the *prakaraṇasama* (the "equal to the point at issue"), he first states the actual state of affairs, saying: "That is not so.
Regarding the phrase "in the end":
it means in the state where no distinction is being apprehended.
But the "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) fallacy has already been explained in the section on the enunciation itself.
And here, the application of one whose time has passed is extremely feeble,
because of the absence of the [proper] time; for he who has no opportunity [to practice], [his application is thus].
When analyzed with respect to its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that [entity] lacks existence;
however, the argument regarding its weaker application is unestablished,
because it is absent by itself at its own time.
But for that which does not exist by its own nature, there is no room for the capacities of contradiction regarding place, time, or state; however,
a weak application constitutes a counter-thesis.
Because for that which exists, there is no occurrence of [specific] states characterized by time and place;
and in the absence of such states, there is no room for either non-contradiction or causal capacity.
Furthermore, a syllogism that allows for such [temporal and spatial] scope is contradictory.
Because [the reason] is contradictory when time, place, and state are present;
for one who argues thus, how can there be any capacity [in the reason]?
Furthermore, the common application [of the reason] is fallible.

The enumeration of the sequence beginning with the "inconclusive" (savyabhicāra) is for the reason that, when there is contradiction regarding time, place, and state, there is a mere absence of capacity [to prove the conclusion].
Alternatively, the inconclusive is easily grasped,
since it is established merely by the proof of its exclusion [from the locus of the probandum].
The establishment of that [fallacy] occurs when a contrary apprehension is demonstrated;
that which is grasped with effort is the *viruddha* (contradictory); that which is grasped with excessive effort is the *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by the context).
Its establishment is achieved by setting aside all other forms that are not it;
[the reason] is difficult to grasp and unestablished,
for some reasons are also unestablished in their locus— this is established by relying on the refutation of the opposing view.

The *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (the "mistimed" fallacy) is more difficult to grasp, because its establishment depends upon first determining the validity of the subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) through its non-otherwise-establishment (*ananyathāsiddhi*). It is with this intention that the order [of the fallacies] is fixed. //4//
// Purity //

Now, in the *Vibhāga-sūtra*, the term "savyabhicāra" (the erratic) was introduced as a mere enumeration (*uddeśa*), yet here the author of the Commentary explains it precisely as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, it might be argued that what was enumerated has not been defined, and what has been defined was not enumerated; to this he says: "And here... (*atra ca*).

Nevertheless, since the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is to be stated, one might ask: "What is the use of the etymological explanation (*padanirukti*) of the term? To this he says: "This is what is meant. That is to say: that which is restricted to one extreme (*ekasminn ante niyataḥ*) means that it is observed to be concomitant (*sahacarita*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) alone, either through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Conversely, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is non-restricted (*aniyata*), meaning it is not observed to be accompanied by the probandum alone.
"Extending to both sides" means, as far as [the term goes], that which results in the application of both sides;
by this, it is clear that the common (*sādhāraṇa*), the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), and the inconclusive (*anupasaṃhārya*) fallacies are included.
He states that the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) resulting from the appearance of cognition is excluded by this explanation: "and it is not of such a nature."
And this will be explained in various places.
"Thus, in this manner" means that the term *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) is to be explained in the same way as the term *anaikāntika*.
"Is it not the case that by this much alone everything has been explained?
What else remains for the sake of which this entire *Vārttika* beginning with 'all this' was composed? To this, he says: "It is understood.
[Objection: But is it not inconsistent [to say] "not indeed other than the object of knowledge (*prameya*)"?
For the two extremes are the probandum and its opposite;
and these do not belong to this [middle way].
Now, this is the meaning:
In that case, this [reason] is not certain either through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Nevertheless, it is not only this one that is of such a nature, for all inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons possess this same character.
Therefore, its exclusion is untenable.

Nor is it correct to argue that there is no fault because [the example] is intended merely as an illustration, since an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*)—such as "both eternal and non-eternal"—is not shown within the category of things to be included (*saṃgrāhyakoṭi*). For this reason, he says: "But of the category of objects of cognition (*prameya-padārtha*)," and so forth.
Thus, this is the meaning of the Vārttika:

some property, such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, belongs to everything; another [property], such as "eternality" (*nityatva*) and so forth, belongs only to a particular thing.

In this context, whatever property— whether it be every property or some particular one— is taken as the reason and applies to the subject by occurring in both extremes, namely the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and its opposite (*tadviparyaya*), that is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

By demonstrating the two-fold nature of properties through the distinction between those that possess negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) and those that lack it, the delimitation of the scope of the inconclusive reason is indicated.
For an inconclusive application is possible only when the property to be proven (sādhya) is one that possesses exclusion (vyatirekin), but not when it lacks exclusion;
yet, was it not previously explained with the intention of [interpreting the term] as a paryudāsa (presuppositional negation)?
To the question, "In that case, how can there be a negation of that? he says: "In the view of paryudāsa."
Nevertheless, "not a non-Brahmin" (*nābrāhmaṇa*) is an example of an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
For people do not say "non-Brahmin" when referring to cows, jars, and the like;
rather, they say it when referring to Kṣatriyas and so forth. He states this with the words "but not," etc., which is easy to understand. //5//
The contradictory [reason] is that which, having accepted a tenet, contradicts it. //6//
// Purity //
He states a verbal defect (*śabdadoṣa*) because the suffix *-ktvā* is untenable due to the absence of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) in the sutra, saying: "Indeed not" (*na khalu*).
He states a semantic defect (*arthadoṣa*), saying: "Nor is it the case that the subject... (*na ca pakṣa*).
And this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
When this [acknowledgment] exists, the points of defeat known as contradiction (*virodha*) and departure from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*) have no scope for occurrence.
Furthermore, if those two were present, even this "contradiction of particulars" (*viśeṣavirodha*) favored by the Mīmāṃsakas would be considered a "contradiction" (*viruddha*).
[The word] "abhyupagama" [means] "acceptance."

The meaning is that by the word *siddhānta* (established conclusion), the "position" (*pakṣa*) is intended here; therefore, there is neither an abandonment of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtahāna*), nor is the fallacy of an unestablished conclusion (*apasiddhānta*) rendered useless.
He wards off the contingency of [the reason] being contradictory to the specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*) with the words "viśeṣa...
By the phrase "having accepted" (*abhyupetya*), it is intended to mean "having proposed as a thesis" (*pratijñāya*).
But it is not "intended" (*abhipretya*).

Nor is a distinction being asserted; rather, it is intended. Furthermore, it is impossible for a contradiction to be perceived with such [an entity] during the stage of non-establishment because it is not perceived, nor during the stage of establishment because it is precluded by the lack of occasion due to its simultaneous perception.
Thus, it is also not tenable to ask how such a thing could even be within the scope of intention.

At the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), because it serves as the means of establishing the subject under discussion, that [general property] is established; however, a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) which does not serve as such a means is not established.
For this very reason, it is also not the object of intention (*abhiprāya*).
Furthermore, one should not ask: "Even then, how can that which has never been perceived in any way whatsoever be established?"

Because, when there is the fulfillment of expectancy and so forth, it is impossible to deny the power of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the communication of a previously unknown object, just as in the case of word-meanings; therefore,
the meaning is that contradiction exists only between two things whose existence is perceived as being restricted by mutual exclusion of their substrates, and not otherwise.
Since it is contradictory to say that something is both "unspoken" and "included," he says: "such is the explanation."
It might be argued: "In the case of contradiction, there can be neither a reason (*hetu*) nor a probandum (*sādhya*).
In the first case, it is simply unestablished (*asiddha*);
in the second, however, it is 'mistimed' (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*)."
What is contradictory now?

Anticipating the objection that [a reason] would be "doubtfully unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddha) even if one of the two [premises] were not certain, the author of the Vārttika stated: "Because it subverts what has been accepted.
It is not unestablished, because it is certain in the subject (pakṣa).
Nor is it a case of the "lapse of time" (*kālātīta*),

because there is no sublation by another stronger means of valid cognition; rather, this very [reason] sublates what is intended to be proven— thus the meaning of the *Vārttika* is indeed easy to understand.
"The second *vārttika* is sublated by what has been accepted.
Even though that [second point] would be unestablished (*asiddha*) if it were sublated by the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*),
nevertheless, where the contradiction itself is prominent, [that is the case].

In that case, one should certainly not point out the "unestablished" (asiddha) nature of the reason— which would require effort to overcome by transgressing [the rule]— because if it were countered by fate (daiva), it would result in the fallacy of "accusing one who should not be accused" (niranuyojyānuyoga); furthermore, since the unestablished nature must be established precisely through the door of the "contradictory" (viruddha), its pointing out is necessary.
This is easy to understand.
However, in accordance with the subsequent Vārttika, he explains it as follows: "The meaning is: either by its own nature or by way of being a logical reason.
Regarding this, there is the Bhāṣya on the example, and so forth.
The meaning is "it has been stated.
The phrase "of the Bhāṣya" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence] regarding the *Antaṣṭīkā*.
Having raised the doubt that this [work] is identical to the *virodha* defeat-condition (*nigrahasthāna*), the manner in which it was resolved by the author of the *Vārttika* is as follows:
It has been explained in accordance with that [principle]. Regarding the state of being based on the proposition (*pratijñāśritatva*),
examples are provided in the Vārttika by means of the extensive treatment of contradictions (*virodhavaibhava*).
In reality, according to our own system, *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets) consists in stating otherwise than what has been established by other means of valid cognition.

*Virodha* (contradiction) is a conflict between two parts of a statement regarding the presence or absence of a single object, resulting in a logical inconsistency (*vyāghāta*). A *viruddha* (contradictory) fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is one that is ascertained to be pervaded by the opposite of the probandum.

And that [inference] for establishing a positive rule (vidhi-sādhana) is of three kinds: non-perception of the essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi), non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi), and perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
For example: "This [place] possesses smoke, because, while being perceptible, it is not perceived as possessing that [fire];
or "because it is devoid of fire."
Regarding the phrase "because it is a body of water":
even in the case of establishing a negation, there are two types of perception—perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvopalabdhi*) and perception of the pervader (*vyāpyopalabdhi*).
For example: "This [place] is without fire..."
Because it is perceived as possessing that [quality], just like "possessing smoke";
and all of this should be understood by way of its qualifiers as well.
For example: "This fire is produced from black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru), because it possesses pungent, foul-smelling, and pale smoke"—this is the summary. // 6 //
That [reason] for which an investigation of the context occurs, and which is put forward for the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion, is the "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) reason. // 7 //
// Purity //

In this context, the results of pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—when considered together with their respective definitions—are, in order: doubt, knowledge contrary to what is intended to be expressed, the desire to know, ignorance, and the sublation of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Among these, the definition of the *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced reason) is now introduced by way of its result, beginning with the words "yasmāt" and so forth.
He explains this very point through the commentary (*bhāṣya*), starting with "prakaraṇa... and so on.
The summary is this: since there arises merely a desire to know the matter under investigation, that is the "equal-to-the-context" (prakaraṇasama) fallacy.
For instance, when an opposing argument proceeds with equal force against a thesis, there is no determination of the truth, because it is obstructed by an equally powerful counter-force.

Nor can there be a sublation of the pervasion (vyāpti) by means of a subsequent [cognition] arising from that [perception], because they possess equal force due to the specific feature being supported [by the perception].
Nor is it simply non-cognition, because its presence in the subject (pakṣa) would entail only one side [of the alternative].
Nor is it contrary cognition (viparīta-jñāna).
Because there is no non-pervasion [of the reason] by that [property],

nor is there doubt, since it does not bring forward both alternatives. Therefore, by bringing forward one alternative while being opposed by an equally strong [reason], it generates the desire for knowledge— namely, "How may a determination be reached here?"— and thus the *prakaraṇasama* (the equal-to-the-issue) is distinguished from the others.

And that state of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) is of three kinds: that which has both reasons established, that which has both reasons unestablished, and that which has both reasons consisting of the established and the probandum.
The first occurs between "not being a substance devoid of form" and "being the locus of a tangible object that is being perceived.
The third occurs between "audibility" and "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).
The middle [position] will be illustrated here;
he explains it in accordance with that, beginning with "He indeed...
Although mere inquiry alone is what is useful here, [he proceeds as follows].
Nevertheless, considering that the persistence or cessation of inquiry follows the persistence or cessation of doubt, it was said: "In that which is doubted, one desires to know that.

Now, one might ask: since the very object of inquiry is [the subject of doubt], how could a discerning person apply themselves toward that very thing for the sake of determining the truth? To this he replies: "Because of the diversity of intentions.

The meaning is that the reasons for employing fallacious means or rejoinders are based on the fact that a previous agreement is difficult to verify and that the intellect of the person being addressed may occasionally be otherwise inclined.
[Objection: But since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is restricted to each individual side, how can there be equality between both sides? To this he says: "This [is that]... [Objection:

If the term *prakaraṇasama* is applied by relying on its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), then what is the use of another definition such as "because of which" (*yasmāt*) and so forth? To this he says: "The etymological derivation... [Objection: Why should this very [derivation] not be the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)? To this he says: "Otherwise..."

In this context, the Commentator, distinguishing the *prakaraṇasama* from the *savyabhicāra*, stated that the former is a cause of doubt while the latter is a cause for the engagement of the debate (*prakaraṇa*). However, that [distinction] remains obscure, because it was previously explained that "the debate consists of the thesis and the counter-thesis" (*pakṣapratipakṣau prakaraṇam*).
Furthermore, it would contradict the Sūtra;
for the Sūtra does not say "from which [comes] the topic" (*prakaraṇa*), but rather "from which [comes] the investigation of the topic" (*prakaraṇacintā*).
Therefore, he says: "The following is what is meant."
Rather, the status of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is due solely to the presence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*).
The sense is that it fails to produce a definitive conclusion because its function is merely to cause a desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*).
By this, it is stated that in the *Bhāṣya*, the word "investigation" (*prakaraṇa*) refers to the desire for knowledge.
Now, is this non-perception of eternal properties intended to be occasional or permanent?
If it is the former, it is indeed inconclusive.
Because even in the case of space and so forth, eternal properties are not perceived at any time.
As for the second [reason], it is simply unestablished;
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove that sound must never possess eternal properties simply because such properties are not perceived.
And since one would not raise the point of "balancing the reason" (*prakaraṇasama*) while abandoning the fault of "unestablishedness" (*asiddhatva*), he says: "Nor is there non-perception of reality.
The meaning is this:
for one who has such a grasp of the distinction, [the following applies].
Let it be that for him this [reason] is indeed unestablished;

however, as for one who— considering non-apprehension to be easily obtained through the mere absence of apprehension— presents a probans by force, without connecting it to a specific [condition] or a necessary connection (*pratibandha*),
should that [probans] be considered fallacious or not?
It does not fail to proceed; for if that were the case, it would establish [the object].
And in this way, the second [cognition] as well, having not apprehended any distinction from that [first], would certainly establish it too.
But this is not the case; nor is that which does not appear [to consciousness] a means of proof, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does any other defect manifest at that time here, except for the obstruction caused by a counter-argument.
Even in cases where multiple defects manifest simultaneously, one desists after having pointed out even the presence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*);
for it is not necessary to point out every single defect that exists.
This is because, elsewhere, there is a rule that [a cause] must be manifested only when it is combined with a formal proposition (*pratijñā*).

Even though, like perception (*pratyakṣa*), the non-apprehension of reality (*tattvānupalabdhi*) is not sufficient by itself, but rather becomes a cause of doubt only when accompanied by the observation of common characteristics (*samānadharmadarśana*) and so forth.

And thus, there is a loss of the desired position for one who is skilled in raising objections; nevertheless, setting that aside, he refutes [the objection] in accordance with his own established tenet: "For not of those that are causeless," etc.
[The opponent asks: "But [is it not the case that] both..."?
In one case, the understanding of the formal argument (*phakkikā*) arises by omitting both terms; in the other, it arises by supplying a term through the door of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
However, the remainder [of the point] is this: the non-perception of reality as stated by us is indeed the example of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy.

Thus, because there is an absence of the cause for inquiry (*jijñāsāhetu*), and due to the lack of connection with the definition of the "neutralized" fallacy, the state of being other than the body is not an example of that [fallacy]; so it has been said.
Now, because it lacks the characteristic of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to being a cause for doubt,
he says "for this reason as well" (*itaśca*), intending that this very [reason] is the illustration of that.
However, some think:

The non-apprehension of the [probandum's] reality (*tattvānupalabdhi*) itself is merely another fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), namely "the counter-balanced" (*prakaraṇasama*); its refutation indicates that other [fallacies] are likewise [to be understood].

When no distinction is being apprehended between two non-apprehensions or between two other properties, there is no difference; however, when a distinction is being apprehended, just as one [property] is included within another fallacious reason, so too is non-apprehension—therefore, it too must be abandoned.
Furthermore, there can be no absolute non-perception of a difference between two non-apprehensions.

For if both were established, it would follow that a single entity possesses the nature of being both [existent and non-existent]. Alternatively, if one were not established, how could there be an absolute non-perception of difference between the two? Moreover, if the reality of both were unestablished, it would again follow that the entity possesses the nature of being both [existent and non-existent]. // 7 //
That which is not distinguished from the probandum, because it is itself yet to be proven, is the "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama). // 7 //
// Purity //
Therefore, because it is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), it is unestablished (*asiddha*).
By way of being that which is to be proven, it is unestablished.
That which is not distinct from the thing to be proven is "not distinct from the thing to be proven" (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).
And that "unestablishedness" (asiddhatā) belongs to something—this and so forth is easy to understand.
Thus, for the sake of the student's ease of comprehension, there is this elaboration of the statement;
but in reality, the definition stated is merely this: "the unestablished is equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).

The meaning of "unestablished" (*asiddha*) is that [the reason] is not ascertained as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Being the object of the final reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) constitutes being a property of the subject;
and this consists in the connection of that which has an unconditioned relation with its own probandum to the subject.

Nevertheless, it is ascertained by the ascertainment of the two related entities accompanied by the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). However, if any one among the pervasion, the logical mark (*liṅga*), or the subject (*pakṣa*) is not ascertained, [the reason] does not [function]. In that regard, due to the non-ascertainment of the subject, it is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Because the probans itself is not ascertained, it is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*);
because the pervasion is not ascertained, it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).
And the non-ascertainment of these occurs either through doubt, or...

Or, because there is certainty regarding non-existence, there is no distinction whatsoever with respect to the result; by this, cases such as "the sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus" are also subsumed. Otherwise, this would not be obtained by the definition: "that which is non-existent in the subject (pakṣa)."
For just as a negation cannot be made when neither a similar instance (sapakṣa) nor a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) exists, so it is with respect to the subject (pakṣa) as well.
"Only when they exist" means "when they are accepted as existing by means of truth."
If it is argued that this [reason] is unestablished because of its lack of permanence, we say no;

for permanence is established by the very fact of being perceived only at certain times. This is because, even when their manifesters are diverse, there is a rule of non-perception for those things related to the manifestation as long as there is no perception of the manifestation itself.
Alternatively, because reality is untenable upon perception,
and because it would follow that [the object] must always be perceived;
if it is argued that this is not so because it is overwhelmed by light— no, [that is not correct].
Because they are not perceived when their substratum is not perceived;
for if that [substratum] were perceived, it would follow that they too would be perceived.
For this very reason, light does not manifest them.
Therefore, at times, perception itself excludes its [the universal's] nature as a generality;
nor is it action.
For action, which separates its own substrate from a previous location and causes it to reach another location, is established in that very state [of change].
It cannot be otherwise,
because the conventional usage of "movement" is not without cause, and there is no other possible cause.

Furthermore, because shadow follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of such objects, its very substratum is not even perceived, let alone its separation from or conjunction with that [substratum]; this is the meaning.
[And] "it is not a quality, because it does not inhere in a substance."
For [a quality] must either be non-inherent in a substance, or inherent in that which is not a substance,
or indeed be non-inherent altogether; in both cases, there is a contradiction with its being a quality.
Because that which possesses a universal would result in being a substance as an independent entity;
and because that which lacks a universal contradicts the definition of a quality, for it is stated: "A quality is that which possesses a universal but is not itself a quality," and so forth.

The meaning is that since qualities and actions are themselves devoid of qualities, it is contradictory for a quality to inhere in them; therefore, if such a quality were to inhere there, it would necessarily follow that it is of the nature of a universal (sāmānya).

He establishes the reason by stating "because of non-inherence in substances": "It is not the mind," because those [substances] lack specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), this must therefore be a general quality (sāmānyaguṇa).

And thus, since there is a rule that the apprehension [of the cognition] is simultaneous with its substratum, if that [substratum] were not perceptible, it would follow by necessity that [the cognition] itself is not perceptible; this is the meaning.
Nor is it a quality of the self (*ātman*).
For this perceptibility by external organs is pervaded by co-referentiality with "this-ness" (*idantā*);
thus, when [the property] ceases upon taking on the status of being a quality of the self, it comes to rest in the state of not being a quality of the self—this is the meaning.
Nor [is it so] for space and air.
For visual qualities are pervaded by their inherence in a material substance;
and that quality of being material, by being excluded from space and air, also excludes their connection with visual qualities—this is the meaning.
Nor can it belong to fire, for being a quality of that [fire] is pervaded by its non-contradiction with the cognition [of the fire];
otherwise, if the possessor of the quality were an obstacle to the cognition of its own quality, it would follow that the quality could never be perceived,
since perception would be contradicted even when inherence exists.
The meaning is that because [the universal] does not exist in the absence of inherence,
its exclusion from that [substratum] also excludes its status as a quality of it;
furthermore, this is because no other quality co-occurring with it is perceived.
The meaning is this:
shadow is not a color-form (rūpa) of light, because this [latter] color-form is necessarily restricted to being white and luminous;
nor is it like the color-form of the luster of a sapphire, because it does not manifest its own substratum.
Therefore, it must be stated that this is indeed a distinct quality belonging to it;
and thus, what is perceived by the eye cannot be perceived without being included within the category of color (rūpa),
because the capacity of the eye is understood to function in precisely that manner.
"From this very reason" means:
first of all, because it is perceivable by the eye alone, shadow cannot even be suspected of being a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*).
Form, however, might be possible;
and that form, being perceived, is pervaded by coldness, fluidity, and so forth as found in water, because it cannot be water if it does not possess those qualities.
Earth, however, is pervaded by perceptible odors and so forth,
because it is impossible for that which is not such [to possess] the nature of earth.
And since that [nature of earth] is concomitant with coldness, odor, and so forth, its cessation— due to non-perception— also brings about the cessation of its status as possessing those qualities.
Moreover:
for it has been established that the capacity of the eye to grasp the color of non-luminous substances belongs only to that eye which is pervaded by external light.
And when something possesses a capacity only when conjoined with another, it cannot perform that function in the absence of that other.
The meaning is that, if that were the case, even damp fuel devoid of fire would produce smoke.
But since the contradiction is even more pronounced, he says: "In that case, however...
By this, the view that darkness is a superimposed terrestrial color is refuted;

for in the absence of external light as a cooperative cause, the eye lacks the capacity for such a superimposition. Indeed, only that [color] which exists elsewhere could be superimposed upon another substratum, like the yellowness of bile.
Or, when it is perceived in that very place or in a restricted location, there is the notion of its being in an unrestricted location—just as something nearby may appear large even when it is minute.
In either case, that [notion] is impossible without first [perceiving the object itself], because it must be superimposed upon one thing while having another as its locus of superimposition.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the eye lacks the capacity to perceive form without light.
Furthermore, an error cannot arise unless both the superimposed object and the locus of superimposition are manifested;
nor can the eye, while inactive with respect to either one of the two, produce an error;
and this cognition is not non-visual.
Because its positive and negative concomitances are not established otherwise;

Nevertheless, there is no exclusion of a valid refutation, because that too consists in a counter-position (pratyavasthāna) by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the reason or by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) with a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Therefore, he says: "And not...

In the commentary, he demonstrates the purpose for explaining the term *jāti* (quibble): "For in debate (*jalpa*), etc. (18).
Misapprehension and non-apprehension are points of defeat. //19//

Since the entire discourse is sealed by the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) itself, its mention later is for the sake of the meaning [of the context]. Intending to show how this follows from the connection of the subject matter, he cites the aphorism: "The Brahmin... (NS 5.2.20). // 19 //
Although, in the discourse on worldly convention, the fault of the person alone constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
for it is the one who has erred who incurs defeat, punishment, and humiliation;
elsewhere in the world, there is merely physical ridicule.
In debate, however, there is merely the pointing out of a transgression;
otherwise, the two disputants have freedom of action.

And a transgression in debate consists precisely in a temporary lack of knowledge regarding reality, which culminates in either a misconception (*vipratipatti*) or a failure to respond (*apratipatti*).
Nevertheless, because its nature cannot be manifested [directly],

and because it is impossible for it to stand in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with terms such as "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) or "incoherent" (*apārthaka*), the Sūtra has been explained as an indication of the means by which that [nature] is inferred.
Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that when a debate has commenced, a move that makes known the opponent's lack of knowledge of reality is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

And this is easily understood by examining the words and their meanings in the context of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "abandonment of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth; furthermore, it is clear from observing the *Vārttika* which demonstrates that [the point of defeat] can be pointed out in its own form.
It will also become manifest immediately thereafter in the *Bhāṣya*.
It might be argued that there is no "deficiency" other than the deficiency of understanding; to this he says: "subtle," etc.
How can this be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? How can it be a point of defeat by its mere existence, while not being perceived in its own nature?
The meaning is that an assault on another's wife which is not even perceived cannot suffice for punishment.
Regarding the term "one who acts wrongly" (*vipratipadyamāna*): it is because one who acts wrongly becomes subject to defeat.

Therefore, it can be understood by way of the attainment of defeat (*parājaya*). Now, what exactly is this attainment of defeat? To this it is said: "The points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), such as the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth, are indeed clearly the attainment of defeat"—the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is that this is self-evident.

Although both misconception (*vipratipatti*) and non-comprehension (*apratipatti*) are possible in the case of an excess [of statements], they cannot constitute points of defeat if those two are absent, because in their absence, the status of being a point of defeat would be untenable.

Nevertheless, the meaning is that the compound was not formed in order to dispel the misconception that [the *adhika*] is not a point of defeat (*anigrahasthāna*), because its object is a matter of conflicting views (*vipratipanna-vastu*).
The mention of "that which is called *adhika*" (*adhikaṃ nāma*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood to include "repetition" (*punarukta*).
Or "corruptible" (dūṣya); the word "or" (vā) is used with reference to future circumstances. // 19 //

Therefore, he says: "according to the definition," which means "according to the essential nature" (*yathāsvarūpam*).

The meaning is that because it is established by scripture (*śruti*) as being for the sake of a specific purpose, there is no lack of consistency with the context (*prakaraṇa*). The remainder of the commentary is easily understood. "Kīrtita" means that which is proclaimed (*kīrttyate*).
And thus, the meaning is that it is easy to understand because the connections are made according to what is appropriate.
Because it is easily grasped by the dull-witted from within the hollows of the ears—being light and as delicate as a flower—it is easy to comprehend even without prior practice;
yet this mind, though now repeatedly at peace, still seems to tremble again and again at the outpouring of the elegant compositions of the illustrious Vācaspati. (20)
